hello.note: Polite, for anyone. The reply is وعليكم السلام (wa a-LEE-kum s-sa-LAAM). Friends just say سلام (sa-LAAM)

how-are-you.note: Literally "no harm on you?", the everyday greeting, the same for anyone. Often just لاباس؟ (la-BAAS)

im-well.note: Literally "no harm, thank God", the same for a man or a woman

good-morning.note: The reply is صباح النور (sbaah n-NOOR), morning of light

good-night.note: Said when parting at night, to a man. To a woman, tes-BAH-ee a-la KHEER. Good evening is مسا الخير (msa l-KHEER)

goodbye.note: Literally "with safety". You will also hear the French au revoir

please.note: To a man. To a woman, a-FAA-kee (عافاكي). It also gets a waiter's attention

thank-you.note: Warmer: بارك الله فيك (ba-RAK l-LAAH FEEK), God bless you. Merci is used too

yes.note: واخا (WAA-kha), OK, is heard all day long

no.note: To a persistent seller: لا، شكرا (la, SHUK-ran), with a smile, and keep walking

excuse-me.note: Sorry, or excuse me to get past, said to a man. To a woman, SMAH-ee LEE-ya (سمحي ليا)

my-name.note: The same for a man or a woman. The audio uses Peter as the example name

where-from.note: Said to a man. To a woman, mneen NTEE (منين نتي؟)

its-beautiful.note: بزاف (b-ZAAF) means very or a lot, and goes after the word

dont-understand.note: The same for a man or a woman

repeat.note: Said to a man. To a woman, A-wdee, a-FAA-kee

speak-english.note: To a man; to a woman, ka-t-HED-ree. French is far more widely spoken than English: كتهضر الفرنسية؟ (l-fran-SEE-ya)

two.note: Moroccan for two. زوج (zoozh) is heard too

thousand.note: Prices are in dirhams (DH). Careful: many people, above all in markets, count in ryal, 20 to the dirham, so ألف ريال is 50 dirhams. If unsure, ask بالدرهم؟ (bed-DER-hem), in dirhams?

how-much.note: Literally "for how much, this?" Point at the thing

would-like.note: Literally "give me ..., please", the usual polite way to order. The audio uses واحد القهوة (WAA-hed l-QAH-wa), a coffee, as the example

i-want.note: Literally "I wanted", and polite enough, the same for a man or a woman. The audio uses هادا (HAA-da), this one, as the example

do-you-have.note: واش (wash) turns a sentence into a question. The same for anyone. The audio uses أتاي (a-TAAY), tea, as the example

just-looking.note: The same for a man or a woman. Useful in the souk

discount.note: Literally "what's the last price?" Haggling is expected in the souks: start low, stay friendly, and walk away politely if it's too much

card.note: La carte, from French. Souks, small shops and taxis want cash

bill.note: L'addition, from French, is understood everywhere

reservation.note: In hotels the French word is more common: عندي ريزيرفاسيون (AN-dee ree-zer-va-SYOON)

checkout-time.note: Literally "when do I have to leave?", the same for a man or a woman

breakfast.note: Literally "is breakfast inside?" Riad breakfasts often come with msemmen pancakes, honey and mint tea

wifi.note: ديال (dyal) means of, and is used all the time

toilet.note: فين (FEEN) means where. From French toilettes

taxi.note: Said to a man; to a woman, AY-tee. A petit taxi drives in town and should use its meter (le compteur); a grand taxi goes between towns and is shared

train.note: From French train. Trains are run by ONCF, and the fast Al Boraq links Tangier and Casablanca

bus.note: A city bus. A long-distance coach is الكار (l-KAAR)

bus-station.note: The coach station. CTM and Supratours have their own, often near the centre

which-train.note: ل (l) means to, and joins the front of the place. The audio uses مراكش (mer-RAA-kesh), Marrakech, as the example

buy-ticket.note: Many people say لبيي (l-bee-YEE), from French billet

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Marrakech as the example

trip-length.note: Literally "how much does the road to ... take?" The audio uses Marrakech

allergic.note: Literally "I have an allergy to", the same for a man or a woman. Add the food: الحوت (l-HOOT) fish, الكاوكاو (l-ka-wa-KAW) peanuts, البيض (l-BEED) eggs. The audio uses peanuts

love-dish.note: Literally "this food pleased me a lot", the same for anyone

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.note: For more people: لتلاتة (l-TLAA-ta), 3, or لربعة (l-RB-a), 4

menu.note: From French menu. La carte is understood too

beer.note: Only licensed bars, restaurants and hotels serve alcohol. Casablanca and Flag Spéciale are the local beers

coffee.note: A نص نص (nuss nuss), half and half, is a small coffee with milk

tea.note: Mint tea, sweet and poured from high up, the drink of welcome. Ask for it بلا سكر (bla SKER), without sugar, if you like

water.note: Drink bottled water. A bottle is قرعة ديال الما (QER-a dyal l-MA)

sugar.note: بلا سكر (bla SKER) means without sugar

hot.note: Hot, of food, drinks and weather. Spicy is حار (HAAR)

cold.note: Cold, of food, drinks and weather

cheers.note: Literally "to your health", the same for anyone. Also said to someone enjoying a meal or new clothes

help.note: Shout it. The police are on 19 in towns; from a mobile, 112 also works

need-doctor.note: For an ambulance, call 15. Doctors often speak French

pharmacy.note: From French pharmacien. At night, look for the pharmacie de garde, the one on duty, listed in every pharmacy window
